entities.name: Uzana of Pagan
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Uzana, who reigned as king of the Pagan dynasty of Burma (Myanmar) from 1251 to 1256, ascended to the throne under the regnal name "Śrī Tribhuvanāditya Dhammarājajayasūra" (ၐြီတြိဘုဝနာဒိတျဓမ္မရာဇᱡယသူရ). His brief five-year tenure marked a period of increasing internal fragility within the Pagan Empire, a once-dominant Buddhist kingdom in Southeast Asia. As the son and successor of King Kyaswa, Uzana inherited a kingdom already showing signs of decline, characterized by a weakening central authority and the growing power of local chieftains and religious institutions. His reign is often viewed as a transitional phase leading directly to the ultimate collapse of the dynasty a few decades later.

Uzana's rule was largely uneventful in terms of grand conquests or significant reforms, primarily due to its brevity and the pre-existing internal strife. He spent much of his time away from the capital, reportedly indulging in hunting, a pastime that ultimately contributed to his demise. The most significant event during his reign was the growing influence and eventual rebellion of his own son, Narathihapate, who would later become the last effective king of Pagan. This dynastic instability, a hallmark of the mid-13th century Pagan, saw royal authority diminish as regional lords and the sangha (Buddhist monastic order) accrued considerable land and power, further decentralizing the state.

Uzana's death in 1256, purportedly from a hunting accident near the city of Bagan, paved the way for the tumultuous reign of Narathihapate. While Uzana himself did not instigate the empire's downfall, his inability to consolidate power or reverse the centrifugal forces at play ensured that the Pagan state continued its trajectory towards disintegration. His reign thus serves as a critical, albeit minor, chapter in the narrative of Pagan's decline, directly preceding the era of Mongol incursions that would irrevocably alter the political landscape of Burma.
